about: Flawed anchor decks: small single-file decks on invented topics, built from the skill's skeleton, engine and the paper-green/editorial theme and its embedded fonts, each carrying one or a few deliberate flaws. With no presenter-scored calibration set, they are how an eval run catches a lenient judge or a broken gate: a judge or gate that passes a must_fail criterion on its anchor is wrong, and one that fails a must_pass criterion is over-strict. Run them through the same gates and judges as any deck, with the same isolation: judges see the deck only, never this file. Sources cited in the decks are invented and use reserved example domains; judge them as cited sources, not as placeholders. The decks hold no comment or name that gives the flaw away; the labels live only here. Regenerated from the skill's development tests after an engine, skeleton or token change.

verdict_rule.must_fail: binary criterion: verdict fail on at least one step, slide or size it judges; scale criterion: score at most 2
verdict_rule.must_pass: binary criterion: verdict pass at every step, slide and size; scale criterion: score at least 3

anchors.name: Clean
anchors.where: whole deck: lead (a0-1, ambient), narrated diagram (a0-2, steps 0–2), quote (a0-3), next steps (a0-4)
anchors.description: A short, clean deck that should pass everything it is checked for: finding titles, a step-built diagram with narration tiles beside the parts they narrate, a verbatim quote with its cut marked and the full wording in the note, every note linked to a source, ambient motion only on the lead slide. A judge that fails it is over-strict.

anchors.name: Short-wide collision
anchors.where: a1-1, steps 1–2, at 1288×598 only: the caption is drawn over the Station dock tile
anchors.description: A fixed-aspect diagram with a caption pinned to the slide's foot. At 1920×1080 and 1280×720 they clear each other; in the short-wide window the caption lands on the lower diagram tiles. Catches gates and judges that only look at one window size.

anchors.name: Low-contrast body text
anchors.where: a2-1 and a2-2, every step: body text in the tertiary ink role at small size (about 3.3:1 on paper)
anchors.description: Body copy and bullets set in the tertiary ink colour at the small type size, well below 4.5:1 on the paper background and faint after screen-share compression. Titles and kickers keep normal contrast, so a judge must look at the body text.

anchors.name: Hook and multi-sentence titles
anchors.where: titles of a3-1 (rhetorical question), a3-2 (teaser), a3-3 (two sentences with full stops), a3-4 (pun, two italics, full stop)

provenance.cite: patterns from the rejected-title column of the presenter voice profile (voice/profiles/twm.md)

anchors.description: Every title is in a form the voice profile rejects: a rhetorical question, a teaser, two short sentences with full stops, and a pun with two italic runs and a trailing stop. The bodies and notes are plain and sourced, so only the titles should fail.

anchors.name: Unsourced figures and a paraphrased quote
anchors.where: a4-1: litre figures and the percentage with no source on the slide or in its note; a4-2: the quoted words differ from the verbatim minutes given in the note
anchors.description: The first slide states figures whose note explains them but cites nothing. The second shows, in quotation marks and attributed, a paraphrase of a sentence whose verbatim wording sits in the note with a linked source, so the mismatch is checkable from the deck alone.

anchors.name: Crammed slide, step list restating a sparse diagram
anchors.where: a5-1, steps 1–3: numbered step list, caption, diagram panel and quote column squeezed into one viewport

provenance.cite: reference deck docs/PRD.md · Design intent, Quality bar, and Workstreams row 6 (first draft rejected, presenter, 20 Nov)

anchors.description: Reproduces the structure of the rejected first draft on a generic topic: a two-line title over a numbered step list that names each diagram node in prose, small nodes floating in a large empty panel, a caption and a column of three quotes, all in one viewport. Nothing collides, so a geometry gate passes it; judges must catch the clutter and the restatement.

anchors.name: Quote tiles far from their nodes and over the title
anchors.where: a6-1, steps 1–3: a fixed column of quote tiles at the left, over the title's second line, while the nodes they narrate appear at the right

provenance.cite: reference deck docs/PRD.md · Workstreams row 6 (first draft rejected, presenter, 20 Nov) and Design intent, Narration tiles

anchors.description: Reproduces the rejected first draft's narration on a generic topic: each step's quote is stacked in a rigid left-hand column far from the ferry or pier it speaks about, and the column starts over the title, hiding part of it.

anchors.name: Accent colour as text
anchors.where: a7-1: the large figure and its lede; a7-2: bullet markers; all in the decorative accent green (about 2.05:1 on paper)

provenance.cite: the palette's rule that the accent is decorative and never text (design/TOKENS.md)

anchors.description: The decorative accent colour is used for a headline figure, its explanatory line and bullet markers. The palette declares the accent never-text, and it misses contrast even for the large figure.

anchors.name: Ambient motion behind a diagram
anchors.where: a8-2, every step: drifting ambient orbs behind the step-built diagram (the lead slide a8-1 has none)
anchors.description: The ambient orb layer, meant only for title, summary and insight pages, drifts behind a step-built process diagram, while the lead slide that could carry it is still. Everything else on the slide is clean.

anchors.name: Reader note with a bare-text source
anchors.where: a9-1: the note names its survey in plain text with no link; the slide's 58% figure has no traceable source
anchors.description: The survey figure's reader note ends with a plain-text source line and no hyperlink, so the claim cannot be traced. The second slide's note is correctly linked, so a judge must check each note rather than the deck as a whole.
